Hey, my realtor just mentioned something about needing to set up an escrow account for my house purchase here in Toronto. I've never dealt with this before, can you explain what escrow actually is and why it's used during the closing process?

Escrow is essentially a neutral third party holding money or documents during a real estate transaction — think of it as a security deposit that neither the buyer nor seller can touch until all conditions of the deal are met. In Toronto, your deposit (typically 5% of the purchase price, though it's often paid directly to the seller's brokerage as a deposit in trust rather than through a formal escrow company like in the US) gets held safely until closing day, when funds are transferred and keys change hands.

The reason it exists is simple: it protects both sides. You don't want to hand over tens of thousands of dollars directly to a stranger who might not complete the sale, and the seller doesn't want to hand over keys to a buyer who might not have the funds ready. Escrow ensures nobody can run off with the money mid-deal.

One thing worth knowing: in Ontario, the closing process is handled a bit differently than in the US — your lawyer typically manages the funds transfer through a trust account rather than a traditional escrow company, so "escrow" in the Canadian context often just refers to the deposit held in trust. Your lawyer will also handle title transfer, registration, and the final money movement on closing day.

That makes sense, so it's basically just a way to make sure nobody gets cheated. What happens if something goes wrong with the house inspection or the financing right before closing? Does the money just sit there in that trust account until the whole thing is sorted out, or is there a specific process for getting it released?

Good news first: in Ontario, the standard OREA Agreement of Purchase and Sale includes conditions like financing and home inspection, and if those conditions aren't met by the deadline, you can walk away and get your deposit back — though you'll need to sign a mutual release with the seller to formally end the deal. The deposit sits in the brokerage's trust account the whole time, untouched, until either the deal closes or the release is signed.

Here's where it gets trickier: if the seller refuses to sign the mutual release (say, they think you're backing out without a valid reason), the money stays frozen in trust until you and the seller resolve the dispute. That can mean negotiation between lawyers, or in worst-case scenarios, paying the deposit into court so a judge can decide who's entitled to it. This is rare, but it's why you want your conditions written clearly with firm deadlines.

One practical tip: if your financing falls through or the inspection turns up something scary, don't just go silent — get your realtor and lawyer involved immediately to document everything and request the release properly. Okay, so it's basically a neutral middleman. I'm just a bit nervous about the "frozen" part. If there's a disagreement and the money is stuck in that trust account, it sounds like it's just being guarded by a third party. Does that third party just sit on the funds, or is there any risk of the money being mismanaged or "lost" while it's just sitting there waiting for a decision?

That's a fair worry, but the risk is genuinely low — brokerage trust accounts in Ontario are heavily regulated. Real estate brokerages must keep client deposits in separate trust accounts, separate from the brokerage's own operating funds, and they're audited by RECO (the Real Estate Council of Ontario). On top of that, deposits are protected by RECO insurance, so even in the freak scenario where a brokerage goes under or someone misappropriates funds, you're covered.

The bigger "risk" isn't theft or loss — it's opportunity cost. While your deposit sits in trust, it's typically held in an interest-bearing account, and here's a quirk: the interest earned on deposits actually goes to RECO, not to you or the seller. You don't lose your principal, but you don't earn anything on it either. That's just how the system works in Ontario.

So the realistic worst case is that your money sits safely but unproductively while a dispute gets sorted out — annoying, but not dangerous. The frozen funds scenario is genuinely rare, especially if your conditions are clearly written with firm deadlines. Keep your paperwork tight, respond quickly to deadlines, and you'll almost certainly never see the inside of a dispute.
